about: Spoken-register guidance for voice agents, per call language and business type. AI-drafted 10 Oct 2026 and expanded 11 Oct 2026 (founder decisions 3, 10 Oct, and the 11 Oct spoken-style rules). EVERY entry here is needs_native_review except prompt_examples (founder approved 14 Oct 2026, see its note): the founder reviews them on the admin screen Ops > Spoken style, whose published edits are stored in the database and layered over this file (calevate_shared.spoken_style.install_published). What each part is for: register is the one-line description of how the language is spoken; word_swaps pairs a formal or written form (left) with what people actually say (right), and the ones named in prompt_swaps go into every agent's prompt in that language, while the whole list guides the script writer, the test callers and the test checks; fillers are the spoken tags and light fillers people use; number_rules and punctuation say how numbers and sentences are written for a voice; examples are example exchanges per business type that show HOW to speak, never facts (no price, time, address or stock level, so an agent cannot repeat a made-up fact); openings are a starter's greeting; spelled_address is how an agent whose caller follows along on a screen spells a web address (D-906): each letter by its English name in the language's letters, a comma between, so a spelled letter is not heard as a word of the language. SCRIPT (founder, 23 Oct 2026, D-861, reversing the 11 Oct English-letters rule): every spoken line is written wholly in the language's own letters, English words and amounts too (కాల్, డెలివరీ, వన్ ట్వంటీ రూపీస్; कॉल, डिलीवरी), after the founder heard a competitor's agent written that way as very human-sounding on Cartesia; every line rewritten to that rule is needs_native_review. Telugu went back on 20 Nov 2026 (founder, after a Varsha call where call and app were misread): Telugu words in Telugu letters, English words and amounts in English letters; Hindi is unchanged. Register sources for te-IN: Telugu has a literary register (grandhika) and a spoken standard (vyavaharika, the sishta vyavaharika of educated everyday speech), the latter championed by Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gidugu_Venkata_Ramamurthy; https://www.deccanchronicle.com/lifestyle/culture-and-society/telugu-language-day-commemorates-gidugu-revolutionary-behind-simple-telugu-usage-1983163). Telugu-English code-mixing ('Tenglish') is extensively used in Hyderabad (Dutta and Rajeswari, Texas Linguistics Forum 2015, https://asol.ling.utexas.edu/salsa/proceedings/2015/Dutta.pdf); Standard and Telangana Telugu differences and code-mixing in speech are studied in Sravani, Kameswari and Mamidi 2021 (https://aclanthology.org/2021.calcs-1.1). Voice facts (Cartesia, read 11 Oct 2026): sonic-3.6 lists Telugu (te); it varies pacing and intonation to the transcript without SSML, pause length adapts to the sentence, and disfluencies such as 'uhm' give a thinking pace (https://docs.cartesia.ai/build-with-cartesia/tts-models/latest); full, punctuated sentences ending in . ? or ! give the best pacing (https://docs.cartesia.ai/build-with-cartesia/sonic-3-5/prompting-tips). Code-switching is documented only for Hindi written in Latin script; Telugu-English mixing is UNVERIFIED in the vendor docs and confirmed only by the founder's ear test ("whole chilli", "call", "kg" spoken naturally). The number style (prices, quantities and times in English words as shop people say them) is the founder's decision of 11 Oct 2026; Cartesia's own guidance would let the model normalise digits, which the founder's ear test overrode for Telugu calls. written_form (F-5, 5 Nov 2026) is one short line the founder writes in the language's own letters the way native speakers write it, suffixes and question particles joined to their word; the in-call written-form rule quotes it, and it stays empty until he writes it.

te-IN.register: Everyday spoken Telugu: vyavaharika, never grandhika; neutral for Telangana and Andhra; Telugu words in Telugu letters, English words in English letters: order, call. అండి and గారు by situation, not in every sentence.

fillers.use: Acknowledging what the caller said or asked for.
Short yes, or showing you are listening.
Mild surprise or 'is that so?' after news from the caller.
A tag asking for agreement: '..., కదా?'
A casual 'what?', as in 'ఏంటి ప్రాబ్లం?'
Before checking something or looking it up.
'I mean' or 'that is', before rephrasing.
Okay, between steps.
A polite yes.
'Sure, will do' to a request.
'Go ahead, tell me' when the caller starts.
'Good' when the caller agrees to a next step.
Sympathy when the caller has a problem: 'అయ్యో, సారీ అండి.'
Reassuring after the caller apologises or declines.

number_rules.text: Prices the English way, as shop people say them: 120 rupees is "one twenty rupees", 250 is "two fifty rupees", 1,500 is "fifteen hundred rupees". Never the rupee sign or digits.
Big amounts as people say them: "seventy lakhs", "one point five crores".
Quantities and units the English way: "one kg", "half kg", "two litres", "two BHK", "twelve hundred square feet".
A time the caller said goes back in the same words: they said "six", say "six". A time you bring up, as people say them: "పొద్దున పది గంటలకు", "మధ్యాహ్నం రెండు గంటలకు", "సాయంత్రం ఐదున్నరకు".
రేపు, ఎల్లుండి and ఈరోజు as they are; weekdays in English as people say them: "Monday", "Saturday".

Phone numbers, OTPs and codes one digit at a time, the English way: "nine eight four nine". A mobile has ten digits: given four, ask for the other six, as in "ఇంకా six digits చెప్తారా?", never read the four back.
Small everyday counts stay Telugu: రెండు నిమిషాలు, ఒక్క సెకండ్; a price or a quantity is said the English way, in English letters.

punctuation.text: Short sentences, one idea each. Split a long sentence into two.
A comma only where the sentence needs one, never in the first sentence of a reply, which is short and whole. The voice speaks a reply in pieces, and an early comma makes the first piece a fragment.
A question mark on every question and a full stop at the end of every other sentence.
No dashes, slashes, brackets, ellipses, quotation marks, bullets or emoji: the voice reads them or stumbles on them.
No dotted abbreviations: "Dr Ravi", never "Dr. Ravi"; say "rupees", never "Rs".
Telugu words in Telugu letters, English words in English letters as written in English: delivery, call, app.
Two choices as two short questions, "whole chilli కావాలా, powder కావాలా?", rather than a list joined with లేదా.

D-894: a reaction only where it fits, so the first answer asks straight on with no opener, and a time the caller said in English words goes back in those words. Wording founder 27 Oct 2026 (the first and third replaced, the second kept), replacing the 23 Oct set whose every turn opened with a reaction. English words in English letters since 20 Nov 2026 (founder, after the Varsha call: call and app were misread in Telugu letters); NEEDS NATIVE-SPEAKER REVIEW. Introduced as how a turn sounds, never words to copy, and carrying no fact. Edited here, not on Ops > Spoken style.
